judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the opening image of the running example. The sentence right before it says 'Consider this image of Ellen Ochoa:', and the Note right after it says that most images in the article deliberately have alt="example image" and that their content is given in the page text. The image's content is named next to it, so a screen reader user loses nothing important. The claim that the alt 'describes something the image does not show' is also wrong: the alt describes nothing at all, and the image really is an example. Rampa's 1.1.1 judge only gets ancestor text, so it saw neither the sentence before the image nor the Note.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Example 1 is a quiz-style exhibit: 'What would you choose as alt text for the image in Example 1?'. The answer text then describes the image ('this is Ellen Ochoa. Her mode of dress further conveys that she is an astronaut'), and the section's Note explains the alt="example image" placeholder. If the article itself is treated as the context, alt="example image" is a placeholder (F30) on an image that WebAIM says carries content, so a strict audit could log it. If the page is treated as a teaching exercise whose content is described in the text (the 1.1.1 test/exercise exception), it passes. Professional auditors would likely disagree on this one. The wording 'describes something the image does not show' is wrong either way, because the image is Ellen Ochoa in an orange flight suit and the alt claims nothing about it.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: This image is the only content of a working link to en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Ochoa, so the link's accessible name is just 'example image'. A functional image's text alternative must convey what the link does, and the page itself says so ('When an image is the only content inside a link or button, alt text is all that a screen reader has to go on'). The didactic Note does not change what a screen reader user gets in a links list: a link called 'example image' that goes to Wikipedia. Strictly, this is a 1.1.1 failure (and it also affects 2.4.4). The message's wording ('describes something the image does not show') is wrong, but the underlying failure is real. The suggested alt is too long and should name the destination, e.g. 'Astronaut Ellen Ochoa'.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the improved version in Example 3. The same link holds the image and the visible text 'Ellen Ochoa, Astronaut', which gives both the content and the link's function. The image is redundant, so its alt adds noise but hides no information (H2: alt="" is the recommended fix, as the page says). The suggested long description would make the redundancy worse. The claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is wrong.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: This is the PDF icon inside the link 'Download the employment application' (Example 4). The link text already conveys the link's function. The icon's only extra information is 'PDF', and that is a demo cue anyway: the link actually goes to an HTML placeholder page (media/generic_link.htm). The exercise text then describes the icon. A strict audit could log alt="example image" because it does not convey the icon's content, while a context-aware audit would accept it as a documented teaching placeholder. The message is wrong as written, because the alt claims nothing false. The suggested 'PDF icon' is the option the page itself calls less appropriate than 'PDF'.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: On this page the separator is not pure decoration. It is the exhibit of Example 5, which the text names directly: 'What alt text would you choose for the horizontal separator image in Example 5?'. The page uses it to illustrate a decorative image, but the finding judges it as if it were a real separator in a real layout. F38 applies to pure decoration only, and this image is the subject of the discussion. The Note explains the placeholder, and the image is fully described in the text, so nothing is lost. Without the article context, the judge mistook a demo exhibit for real decoration.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: This is the Example 6 exhibit. The quiz text names its content ('Handshake', 'Businessmen shake hands to complete a contract'), and the article explains that in the scenario the image adds nothing important. A descriptive alt like the suggested 'Two people shaking hands to symbolize a business agreement' is exactly what WebAIM calls superfluous here. Read as a teaching exhibit, the content is in the text. Read as a stock photo in the scenario, the issue would be 'should be alt=""', not 'too generic'. Either way, the claimed failure and the fix are not what an audit would log.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: Example 7 is Emanuel Leutze's 'Washington Crossing the Delaware'. The text near the image says only 'In this painting, the artist Emanuel Leutze used light, color, form...', and WebAIM itself notes that the content is not (entirely) in the surrounding text. The subject appears only in the quiz options and discussion that follow. A strict audit could log the placeholder alt on this informative image. Treating it as a documented teaching exhibit (the Note, and the test/exercise exception) would pass it. The suggested alt is also inaccurate: it describes 'figures appearing to be in distress or being rescued' on a 'frozen river', when the painting shows Washington and his troops crossing the icy Delaware.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The link text 'images' sits in 'This article is focused on images, but its principles also apply to multimedia...', and it goes to WebAIM's 'Accessible Images' article (/techniques/images). Read with its sentence (link context, G53), the text tells the user it leads to more about images, and that is where it goes. This meets 2.4.4. The suggested 'Accessible Images' only rewords it.

The link text plus its sentence identify the purpose, so this meets 2.4.4. The suggested text uses the destination's title but adds no information a user needs.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The section explains that the same image needs different alt text depending on how it is used ('This image may need vastly different alternative text depending on how it is used'). judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: 'Example 1' is a numbered example inside h2 'Context is Everything'. The text refers to it by that name ('the image in Example 1'), and it contains an example. Under its parent heading, the heading describes its purpose. The Understanding doc says headings can be short and need not be long. The suggested 'Alt text for Ellen Ochoa image' would also be identical to the fix proposed for Example 2.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The footer h2 '©2026 WebAIM' heads WebAIM's footer block, which holds its address at Utah State University and phone number. The heading names the organization the block is about, so it does not 'name a different topic'. Using a copyright line as a heading is unusual, but it is not a 2.4.6 failure, and the suggested 'Copyright Information' describes the block's contents (contact details) less accurately.
